key_insight: Using reverse predictivity (predicting model unit activity from brain responses) reveals that only a minority of ANN units truly align with primate neural responses, exposing a large ANN–brain misalignment despite strong bidirectional alignment between two primate brains.
problem_solved: Clarifies whether high model-to-brain predictivity indicates genuine mechanistic alignment or arises from partial, unit-level correspondences — resolving ambiguity about how well ANNs mirror actual brain computations.
method: Compute bidirectional predictivity: standard forward mapping (ANN → brain) and reverse predictivity (brain → ANN) using cross-validated linear mappings.
Identify and quantify the subset of ANN units that are reliably predicted from primate responses, and compare alignment patterns to primate–primate bidirectional predictivity.
Analyze the distribution of aligned vs. non-aligned units to assess whether alignment is global or concentrated in subpopulations.
impact: Provides a sharper diagnostic for comparing models to brains, guiding practitioners to evaluate alignment at the unit/subpopulation level rather than relying on aggregate forward predictivity alone — informing model selection and architecture design for brain-inspired AI.
visual_elements: Bidirectional diagram showing forward (ANN→brain) vs reverse (brain→ANN) predictivity with partial overlap highlighting aligned units
Bar chart or pie chart quantifying fraction of ANN units with high reverse predictivity versus total units
Scatter plot of forward vs reverse predictivity per unit to show which units are mutually predictable
Side-by-side comparison icon/infographic showing strong bidirectional alignment between two primate brains vs sparse ANN–brain alignment
paper_title: Reverse predictivity for bidirectional comparison of neural networks and biological brains
